Concepts to grasp

Semantic HTMLTags & structure

Plain English

Before any colour or layout, a page is just structure. Instead of using generic boxes everywhere, HTML gives you meaningful tags: <header> for the top bar, <nav> for links, <main> for the main content, <section> for each chunk, and <footer> at the bottom. The names describe the job.

Try it on this page

Turn on Highlight mode below. Every part of this live page gets an outline and label colour — header in red, nav in blue, main in green, sections in gold, footer in grey. Scroll around and spot them.

■ Header — top bar■ Nav — links■ Main — all content■ Section — each block■ Footer — bottom
<header> LUMÉ + nav + Bag </header> <main> <section id="collection"> Perfumes </section> <section id="notes"> Notes </section> </main> <footer> Links + © </footer>

Concepts to grasp

CSS Grid — 2D layoutFlexbox — 1D rows

Plain English

Grid is for big layouts in rows and columns — like the 6 perfume cards. Flexbox is for lining things up in a single row — like the nav links or the buttons inside a card. Most real sites use both together.

Try it on this page

Jump to the live Grid demo in Learn the Build. Change 2 → 3 → 4 columns and watch the boxes re-flow instantly. That's exactly how the product grid works — just with photos.

Open the Grid demo ↓See it in the shop ↑
.grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); gap: 26px; } /* Flexbox inside each card footer */ .card-foot { display: flex; justify-content: space-between; }

Concepts to grasp

CSS VariablesDesign tokens (:root)

Plain English

Imagine changing a button colour in 20 places by hand. Variables fix that. You set --accent once in :root, then everywhere else you just write var(--accent). Change the one line — the whole site updates.

Try it on this page

Use the swatches in Learn the Build. Pick Clay Rose, Mist Blue, Sand — watch the buttons, badges, kickers and this Journey section change together. That's one variable doing all the work.

Try the colour swatches ↓
:root { --accent: #7d8b74; --ink: #26231f; --serif: "Cormorant Garamond", serif; } .btn { background: var(--accent); font-family: var(--serif); }

Concepts to grasp

Events (click)DOM — changing the page

Plain English

JavaScript listens and reacts. An event is something happening — a click. The DOM is the live page JavaScript can change. So: when you click (event), change something on the page (DOM). That's the whole pattern.

Try it on this page

Filters + Search + Sort: try them above the grid — JS checks each card and shows only matches, in the order you choose. Bag: click Add to Bag or Quick View — JS adds the item (with size & quantity) to a cart array, saves it, updates the header counter, and renders the drawer. Try both now, then come back.

Try filters + Add to Bag ↑
// 1. Listen for a click (event) button.addEventListener("click", function() { // 2. Change the page (DOM) bag = bag + 1; bagCount.textContent = bag; });

Concepts to grasp

TransitionsKeyframes + scroll reveal

Plain English

A transition smooths a change — hover a card and it lifts slowly instead of jumping. Keyframes define a full animation from start to finish — like sections fading up as you scroll. Good animation is quiet: it guides the eye, it doesn't shout.

Try it on this page

Toggle animations off, hover a product card and scroll — everything feels flat and instant. Toggle back on and feel the difference. This switch also respects people who prefer less motion.

Animations are currently ON — hovers lift, sections fade in.

.card { transition: transform .35s ease; } .card:hover { transform: translateY(-6px); } @keyframes fadeUp { from { opacity: .15; transform: translateY(14px); } to { opacity: 1; transform: none; } }

Concepts to grasp

Responsive / media queriesAccessibility basics

Plain English

Most visitors are on phones. A media query says “if the screen is small, change the layout” — here the 3-column grid becomes 1 column. Accessibility means everyone can use it: readable contrast, alt text on images, big tap targets, labels that make sense without sight.

Try it on this page

Resize this window narrow (or open on your phone) — cards stack, nav simplifies, text stays readable. Then take the final quiz in Learn the Build to lock in Grid + Variables.

Take the final quiz ↓
@media (max-width: 600px) { .grid { grid-template-columns: 1fr; } /* stack cards */ .nav-links { display: none; } } /* Accessibility: every image has alt text, every button is at least 44px tall to tap */

Fragrance notes

Get to know the notes

Every scent is built from notes — the ingredients you actually smell. Tap one to see what it brings.

Our story

Started at a kitchen table

LUMÉ began with a single question: why does a beautiful scent need thirty ingredients and a shouty bottle? We started blending at home, one note at a time, keeping only what earned its place.

Today each fragrance is still mixed in small batches, rested for two weeks, and bottled by hand. If a scent doesn't make you pause for a second when you first smell it, it doesn't leave the table.

Few notes, done well

Three to five notes per fragrance — nothing hiding, nothing filler.

Small batches

Blended in runs of fifty bottles, so every batch stays fresh.

Made to be worn daily

Soft, close-to-skin scents that suit work, weekends and everything between.

Kind words

Worn and loved

The scent letter

New scents, first

One short email a month — new batches, restocks and the stories behind each note. No noise.

You're on the list — welcome in. ✓

Learn the build

The 2 concepts behind this page

This whole site runs on two CSS ideas. Try them live — nothing here is a picture, it's the real code working.

1 · CSS Grid — lay things out in rows & columns

The product cards above sit in a grid. You give the container one instruction — how many columns — and every card arranges itself. Press the buttons and watch the demo row re-flow. Resize the window and it still behaves.

Columns:
First Light
Petal
Amber Hour
Still
Dune
Rosewater
.grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); /* 3 equal columns */ gap: 26px; /* space between cards */ }

2 · CSS Variables — set a value once, use it everywhere

The sage green on this page's buttons, badges and highlights isn't typed in ten places — it's stored once in a variable called --accent. Tap a swatch: one value changes, and the whole page follows. Scroll up and check the buttons.

Current accent: Sage · #7d8b74

:root { --accent: #7d8b74; /* ← change this ONE line… */ } .button { background: var(--accent); } /* …and this updates */ .badge { background: var(--accent); } /* …and this */ .kicker { color: var(--accent); } /* …and this */

Quick check — 3 questions

Answer from what you just tried above. No pressure, you can re-try any time.

Q1. What does grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr) do?

Right — repeat(3, 1fr) = 3 columns, each one equal fraction of the space. That's the product grid above.

Q2. Where do you define a CSS variable like --accent so the whole page can use it?

Exactly — variables defined in :root are available to every element on the page.

Q3. If you change --accent in one place, what happens?

That's the whole point of variables — one change, everywhere. You just did it with the swatches.
